payload.description:
## Observation
`tests/test_board_serve.py::test_a_stale_lock_hands_the_fold_back_to_the_viewer` failed inside the pre-push suite on 2026-09-12, refusing a docs-only push. The full suite had passed minutes earlier on the same tree.

```
assert None is not None
tests/test_board_serve.py:218: AssertionError
```

Line 218 is `assert served is not None`. Lines 215 and 216 passed, so `board.refresh()` had returned True and `board.refreshes` was 1.

## Not reproduced
Three runs of the test alone: pass. Three runs of the whole file under `-n 8`: 27 passed each time. Six attempts, zero reproductions.

## Hypothesis ruled out, recorded so nobody spends the same hour
The obvious read is a race between the two independent `live_holder` calls: `refresh` proceeds only when the holder is not live, and `payload` returns `_served` only when the holder is not live, otherwise reading a snapshot file that may not exist. That would explain a None.

It cannot happen. `live_holder` returns None once `age_s >= STALE_AFTER_S`, the test ages the lock to `STALE_AFTER_S + 1`, and an age only grows. The holder cannot become live between the two calls.

So `payload` returned `_served` and `_served` was None, while `refresh` had returned True on the branch that assigns it. Those two statements cannot both be true of one object, which is why this needs an instrument rather than another read.

## Suggested first step
Have the test print `board.failures`, `board._served is None` and the holder age at the point of failure, then leave it in the suite until it fires again. A cause guessed without a second observation is a guess.

## Why it matters
The pre-push suite is the gate before every push. A test that fails about once refuses work that is fine and trains people to re-run rather than read. This is the second timing-dependent test in this file: `basicly-gssz1qa` fixed a different one on 2026-09-12, which compared two pages against the clock.

## Scope
- `tests/test_board_serve.py`
- `src/basicly/board_serve.py`

payload.description:
## Context

Three defects in one day, all the same shape: **a consumer reads a snapshot field the producer never writes, and every test on both sides passes.**

| record | the field | how it was found |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `basicly-3qstvw` | `asks[].actions[].basicly` | by grepping the producer after shipping the consumer |
| `basicly-tyobdb` (adjacent) | the gate verdict's age | by the owner misreading the page |
| filed alongside this one | `events[].kind == "status"` | by asking why `CLOSED TODAY` said `not measured` |

Each consumer was correct. Each producer was correct. The **seam** was never asserted, because the fixtures under `tests/fixtures/board/` are written against the *schema*, and a schema is a superset of what the producer implements. So an end-to-end test can serve a document more capable than anything the producer can emit — which is exactly what `tests/test_board_action_wire.py` did while the live board drew no form.

## The gate

For every key the board's consumer modules read out of a snapshot section, either the producer writes it, or the pair is declared as a gap with a reason. Both halves are mechanical:

- the consumer side is a literal-string scan of `src/basicly/board_{wall,regions,footer,loop,diagram,graph,asks}.py` for `.get("<key>")` and `["<key>"]` against a section reading;
- the producer side is the same scan over `src/basicly/board_{snapshot,sections,usage,facts}.py` for the keys it assigns.

A key the consumer reads and the producer never writes is either a defect or a declared foreign-producer affordance. The declaration is the point: `harness-board/v1` is deliberately a contract for producers that are not this harness, so some keys are legitimately unwritten here — and today nobody could tell those apart from the broken ones.

## Acceptance Criteria

## Trigger

When a consumer module in the board reads a snapshot key its own producer never writes, I want a gate that catches the mismatch, so I can tell a real defect from a declared foreign-producer affordance.

## Context

Three defects in one day, all the same shape: **a consumer reads a snapshot field the producer never writes, and every test on both sides passes.**

| record | the field | how it was found |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `basicly-3qstvw` | `asks[].actions[].basicly` | by grepping the producer after shipping the consumer |
| `basicly-tyobdb` (adjacent) | the gate verdict's age | by the owner misreading the page |
| filed alongside this one | `events[].kind == "status"` | by asking why `CLOSED TODAY` said `not measured` |

Each consumer was correct. Each producer was correct. The **seam** was never asserted, because the fixtures under `tests/fixtures/board/` are written against the *schema*, and a schema is a superset of what the producer implements. So an end-to-end test can serve a document more capable than anything the producer can emit — which is exactly what `tests/test_board_action_wire.py` did while the live board drew no form.

## The gate

For every key the board's consumer modules read out of a snapshot section, either the producer writes it, or the pair is declared as a gap with a reason. Both halves are mechanical:

- the consumer side is a literal-string scan of `src/basicly/board_{wall,regions,footer,loop,diagram,graph,asks}.py` for `.get("<key>")` and `["<key>"]` against a section reading;
- the producer side is the same scan over `src/basicly/board_{snapshot,sections,usage,facts}.py` for the keys it assigns.

A key the consumer reads and the producer never writes is either a defect or a declared foreign-producer affordance. The declaration is the point: `harness-board/v1` is deliberately a contract for producers that are not this harness, so some keys are legitimately unwritten here — and today nobody could tell those apart from the broken ones.

## Scope

- `.scripts/check_board_seam.py`
- `basicly.toml`
- `tests/test_check_board_seam.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- demonstration: Delete one key from `board_sections.asks` and watch the gate name it; then restore it and watch the gate pass.

payload.description:
## Context

Three failures on 2026-08-06 were process errors the harness could have prevented, and
two of them recurred *within the same session* — which is the definition of knowledge
that belongs in the repo rather than in a head.

1. **`pgrep -f` / `pkill -f` self-match.** Both match the caller's own command line.
   `pkill -f "loop run <id>"` SIGTERMed the invoking shell (exit 144) while the target
   survived; later an `until ! pgrep -f "loop run <id>"` waiter matched itself, so its
   condition could never become true and it spun for 30 minutes **reporting a job as
   still running that had already succeeded**. The stale report is the damaging half.
2. **Monitoring commands were re-invented per lane** instead of reused, which is how the
   dotted-worktree-name trap (`basicly-jr0l.65` provisions `basicly-jr0l-65`) was
   rediscovered mid-session after it had already been observed.
3. **A valuable artifact was written to the scratchpad and destroyed.** An 846-line design
   document and the agent transcript that produced it both vanished between being written
   and being installed; only the conversation made them recoverable.

## What was done

Both rules landed as **skill** content rather than fragments, because the always-on tier
has no room: `AGENTS.md` measures 11 characters of headroom against its 12000 cap and
architecture already records that the next scoped fragment does not fit. A skill is
on-demand and costs the baseline nothing.

- `harness-loop` gains a *Watching a lane* section: the four canonical read commands, the
  dotted-name rule, the two self-match traps with their exact failure modes, and the rule
  to read a landing from its own summary rather than a filtered tail.
- `session-finish` gains two pickup-clean rules: no background process outlives the
  session, and anything worth keeping goes straight to its final path in the repo.

## What is deliberately not done, and why

No always-on fragment. The measured headroom forbids it, and forcing one in would push
codex over its cap — which is the tier that has no glob scoping and inlines everything.

## Follow-up worth considering separately

A deterministic check could catch the first class outright: a `pgrep -f`/`pkill -f` whose
pattern is not bracket-guarded is mechanically detectable in any shell a hook sees. Not
filed as part of this bead because it needs a home — the harness does not currently lint
the commands an agent runs, only the files it writes.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/skills/harness-loop/skill.yaml`
- `.basicly/core/skills/session-finish/skill.yaml`

payload.description:
Retro finding, session 2026-08-13. Proposed by the agent, not self-applied. Two rejections, three
lost commits between them.

## Context

**1. `br update --status closed` is refused.** Terminal transitions must go through
`br close <id> --reason "..."` so close-policy (close reason, acceptance criteria, attribution) is
enforced. The error names the remedy, but only after the command has failed inside a chained
command - and this repo rule is that a rejected step in a chain leaves the chain half-run.

**2. Any hand-run `br` write re-exports machine-specific absolute paths** into
`.beads/issues.jsonl`, and the `tracker-path-scan` pre-commit hook then blocks the commit naming
hundreds of lines. A `basicly loop advance` repairs it automatically, which is exactly why it only
ever appears on commits made by hand after tracker work done outside the loop. Repair:

```sh
uv run python -c "from pathlib import Path; import basicly.br as b; print(b.scrub_export(Path(.)))"
```

then re-stage. It reports the number of lines scrubbed.

**The diff shape is the tell, and it matters because it mimics a known catastrophe.** Before
scrubbing, a commit filing one bead plus two comments showed as `752 insertions, 752 deletions`;
after scrubbing, `+3 -2`. A whole-file tracker diff reads exactly like the WAL corruption the
skill already warns about, and the two are told apart by comparing the id SETS either side, not
the line counts.

This session hit both. The second fired twice, in the same session in which its remedy had already
been written down elsewhere - which is the argument for it being in the skill rather than in a
note.

## Steps to Reproduce

- Run `br update <id> --status closed` - refused, naming `br close`.
- Run any `br create` or `br comments add`, then `git add .beads && git commit` - the
  `tracker-path-scan` hook blocks with `machine-specific path(s) in the staged tracker export`.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/skills/tool-br/skill.yaml`

## Context

Three decision records rest on premises the tracker flip expired, and one of them was false the day it was written. Everything in T2 to T6 cites the replacement, so this lands first.

**D-28** says a handoff artifact travels as a comment marker, never a ledger append, because the landing advance sweeps base-checkout dirt only under the tracker path. Measured 2026-08-18: `merge.py` calls `commit_tracker_state` and only then `_assert_base_ready`, so ledger dirt is swept before the clean-tree check. `git log -L` dates that behaviour to `b20a0b5a`, 2026-08-15. D-28 was authored in `e0b38e7f`, 2026-08-16. Its reason was carried over from the requirements document, where it correctly named the external store, and the noun was updated without re-running the measurement.

**D-23**, the seam is the only place where both stores move together. There is one store. Its own table row already reads `expires at the flip`. The rule survives with a different reason, which the configuration already names: the read-only guard, the argv classification and the event translation all live at the seam.

**D-35**, the external binary is transitional. It is gone. Section 37 describes it in the present tense throughout and its cutover table still marks the flip step not dispatchable.

**Section 32.10's first rule** claims only free-text keys truncate and never a field the fold reads. The allow-list contains `value`, and the fold reads `value`. One record has already lost 365 bytes of its description permanently.

## The decision to record, D-36

A handoff artifact is one typed `artifact` event in the owned ledger, body under a key the per-event cap does not name, never truncated. Its size is bounded by removing what the ledger can already derive; where nothing is derivable the body is stored whole. D32's branch-file alternative is rejected: its premise expired at the flip, and deleting the body at teardown leaves a digest whose preimage is gone, which proves bytes existed and nothing about what they said. Refusal is also rejected, on three measured grounds carried in the analysis.

The accepted cost is stated, not waved: every artifact body is in every clone forever, measured at 478311 bytes against a 5.7 MB log, about 8 percent.

## Acceptance Criteria

Given the decision table then D-28 reads superseded by D-36 rather than accepted, and D-23 and D-35 no longer read as live.
Given D-28's body then it names the commit and the date its reason expired, and keeps the record rather than deleting it.
Given D-36 then it states the rejected alternatives with their reasons and the accepted permanence cost with its measurement.
Given section 32.10's first rule then it names `value` as the fold-read key the allow-list contains.
Given section 33 then it no longer asserts the marker mechanism as the design.
Given no heading is renumbered then every existing intra-document anchor still resolves.

- `docs/architecture/architecture.md`

- A configured command missing from PATH fails with a one-line message (mirror verify.py's 127/126 contract), never a traceback.
- The authoring repo declares its full check set in its own basicly.toml (adds bandit and markdownlint entries) so dogfood coverage is unchanged — verified by running both hook scripts against this repo.
- Unit tests: empty config passes, failing check fails, missing tool one-liner, mode routing (fast vs full).

[interface-facts 2026-08-31] Vendor event names for the sessionstart stage, fetched today, not recalled.

COPILOT: event name is sessionStart (camelCase). Source: docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/hooks-reference and docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/customize-copilot/use-hooks, both fetched 2026-08-31 (HTTP 200). Schema: .github/hooks/NAME.json, version 1, hooks keyed by event name; a sessionStart entry takes type/bash/powershell/cwd/timeoutSec, default timeout 30 s. Output contract: stdout is parsed as ONE JSON object and only additionalContext is injected, as a prepended user message - plain text is unparseable and dropped without a word. PascalCase SessionStart is the VS Code-compatible alternative, whose payload carries hook_event_name and snake_case fields; camelCase selects the camelCase payload (sessionId, timestamp, cwd, source). Observed firing on 2026-08-31 in a 1.0.82 session debug log: [rust:hooks] [hook stdout] {"additionalContext": "ledger: 1187 records, ...} and the same text in the turn message payload. The model call was then refused for quota, so injection is proven from the log, not from a model answer.

payload.description:
## Trigger

When the engine decides whether to keep a session open for another task, I want the adapter to state its host's prompt cache window, so I can hold that decision on a declared host fact rather than on a constant somebody guessed.

## Requirements

R1. The engine never assumes a cache window a host has not published.
R2. A host that publishes no window is handled, and the handling is visible rather than silent.
R3. A window that the vendor changes is corrected in one declaration, not in every call site.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When a runner spec declares a cache window, then `runner` exposes it beside the context window and names its source. [check: `tests/test_runner.py`]
- When a runner spec declares no cache window, then the engine treats the host as having none and dispatches fresh. [check: `tests/test_runner.py`]
- When a dispatch is recorded, then the run record carries the window that was in force and where it came from. [check: `tests/test_run_record.py`]

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_runner.py -q`

## Design notes

Architecture D-46. The existing `context_window` and `context_window_source` pair on `RunnerSpec` is the shape to copy. Sourced 2026-09-13: the Claude host writes a one-hour cache on the main path and five minutes for an in-process subagent unless `subagentPromptCacheTtl` is set to `1h`.

## Trigger

A consumer wants shared Codex settings that preserve automatic review without globally activating basicly permissions or sharing sibling grants across repositories.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/codex_permissions.py`
- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `src/basicly/runner.py`
- `.basicly/core/permissions/codex-profile.yaml`
- `tests/test_codex_permissions.py`
- `tests/test_cli.py`
- `tests/test_runner.py`
- `docs/how-to/configure-codex-permissions.md`
- `changelog.d/*`

## Plan

Reuse the existing unmerged projector merge logic in an isolated change. Name the shared base basicly-workspace. Use a portable repository-specific derived profile and keep absolute sibling grants only in explicitly registered local user settings. Preserve reviewer and network opt-outs, unrelated settings, and protected metadata. Register via install --codex-user and permissions-build --codex-user. No global reviewer supplement or command rules.

## Evidence

Codex 0.162.1 current official permissions documentation supports absolute/home-relative roots and rejects parent traversal under workspace-relative subpaths. Installed basicly 0.23.1 does not yet ship Codex projection. Existing projection is staged with the Lefthook migration and must not be modified or absorbed.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a lane runner killed by the wall clock with uncommitted changes in its worktree when the loop next advances then that work is committed on the harness branch and judged by the verify gate rather than discarded and re-dispatched as not-ready and the stall decision item is still queued so the timeout remains visible to a human with tests
payload.description:
## Context

Measured 2026-08-06 from `.basicly/usage/run-records.json` at 7bc44d0, after `basicly-m4zv.5`'s
lane died this way. **81 metered claude dispatches, 527,629,368 tokens, 413.95 USD.**

| | runs | tokens | share |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| executed | 68 | 474,355,290 | 89.9% |
| failed | 13 | 53,274,078 | 10.1% (41.99 USD) |
| *of which ran past 1100s* | **3** | **47,784,950** | **90% of all waste** |

Three runs account for nine tenths of every token this repo has spent on work that did not land.
Each was killed by `[runner] runner_timeout` after 20-30 minutes with **complete work sitting
uncommitted in its worktree**, and the harness discarded it - because committing is the *agent's*
last step, and the agent is what got killed.

```
basicly-o8p0     1801s  rc=None  21,517,477 tokens
basicly-m4zv.5   1801s  rc=None  16,387,353 tokens
basicly-kjc5.44  1201s  rc=None   9,880,120 tokens
```

`m4zv.5` is the one we can speak to directly: the work was **finished**, not partial. It passed 500
tests and 16/16 full checks unchanged, and was committed by hand with no edits. So 16.4M tokens
bought a correct change that the harness treated as a failed run.

## This is not the collision class, and fixing that did not fix this

Attempts 1-4 of the `basicly-u6jq.1` proof run failed on **shared-anchor landing collisions**;
`basicly-4746` removed the cause and `basicly-bdd4`/`basicly-m4zv.5` made the recovery converge.
That class is closed. This is a **second, unrelated** class that the same proof run now trips, and
it has no bead - the many "(context-ceiling overrun)" follow-ups are the *context* ceiling, a
different mechanism, already corrected to 1,000,000.

## The ceiling has no margin above the real work

`runner_timeout = 1800` (basicly.toml:292), deliberately below the 3600s default. Against the
measured distribution of *successful* lanes:

- longest success: `basicly-tcmy.34` at **1712s — 95.1% of the cap**
- 10 of 68 successes (15%) finished past 80% of the cap
- 2 of ~71 lanes that got past startup hit the wall clock outright (~3%)

So the ceiling sits inside the upper tail of legitimate work rather than above it. A lane 5% larger
than `tcmy.34` dies, and dies at maximum cost.

## Root cause: one timeout doing two incompatible jobs

The config comment says why 1800 was chosen: *"Lower than the 3600s default while an unsizeable
lane still defeats both dispatch cost gates (basicly-vz78): with no forward forecast, this timeout
is the only per-lane ceiling on a runaway run."*

So a **runaway guard** is standing in for a missing forecast, and it is the same number that bounds
a **legitimately long** lane. Nothing distinguishes them, so the guard cannot be loosened without
un-bounding the runaway case. Raising the number only moves the cliff.

## Fix shape — narrowed to preserving the work

**Scope narrowed 2026-08-06.** This bead originally proposed three steps. Steps 2 and 3 moved to
`basicly-lpsf` (retire the wall clock as the working bound), which is blocked on `basicly-rupz`
because today's activity probe cannot tell a thinking lane from a wedged one. What remains here
needs nothing new and recovers the loss on its own.

**Commit what the worktree holds when a lane is killed.** A timeout is the harness's decision, not
evidence against the diff, and the tree is already on disk. Commit it on the harness branch and let
the landing judge it — **verify is the right authority on a diff; a clock is not.**

Three properties make this the cheap half:

- **Agent-independent.** It needs no cooperation from a third-party CLI. `_kill_tree` terminates
  then SIGKILLs, and any scheme where the agent commits on a signal depends on `claude -p` treating
  SIGTERM as "commit now", which it does not promise. The salvage has to be harness-side.
- **It composes with what already shipped.** Today a killed lane leaves an uncommitted tree, the
  landing refuses `not-ready`, `_route_failed` charges the dispatch cap and re-dispatches — paying
  a second full run for finished work. A commit turns that refusal into a real *finding set*, which
  is exactly what `basicly-bdd4`'s brief and `basicly-m4zv.5`'s convergence check consume.
- **It cannot silently pass off unfinished work.** The commit is judged, not trusted: if verify is
  red the lane reworks with real findings; if green it lands. Either way the tokens bought
  something. Keep the stall queue item either way — a timeout is still a thing a human should see,
  and this bead must not turn one into a silent success.

Deliberately **not** in scope here: raising `runner_timeout` (that is `lpsf`, and alone it just
moves the cliff), and marking the commit in a way that lets ship close the bead without a human
seeing the timeout happened.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Dispatch a lane whose work needs more than `[runner] runner_timeout` seconds.
2. Watch the runner be killed at the deadline (`rc=None`, the run recorded `failed`).
3. Inspect the worktree: the edits are present and uncommitted.
4. Advance the loop. The landing refuses with "commit the work on `<branch>` before landing", the
   dispatch cap is charged, and the lane is re-dispatched - paying a second run for finished work.

Observed on `basicly-m4zv.5`, 2026-08-06, at 16,387,353 tokens.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/runner.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `basicly.toml`
- `tests/test_runner.py`
- `tests/test_supervise.py`
payload.title: A lane killed by the wall clock loses its whole run because it never commits

payload.text:
Investigated the implementation 2026-08-06 at 3269082. **The kill mechanism is not buggy** - it is
a careful piece of work - and saying so matters, because the defect is one layer up and a patch to
the mechanism would miss it.

`runner.run` (runner.py:1030-1056) spawns with `start_new_session` precisely so the dispatch is
killable as a *tree*, and on `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` it sets `timed_out`, nulls the returncode,
calls `_kill_tree` (killpg on POSIX, `taskkill /T` on Windows) and `_drain`s the pipes so buffered
output survives. `RunResult.timed_out` is a distinct field, not a returncode overload, and three
callers branch on it. All correct.

## What is actually wrong: terminal authority is on the uninformative signal

Two mechanisms watch a lane, and they have their powers backwards.

| | measures | knows if work is happening | power |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `runner_timeout` = 1800s | wall clock since spawn | **no** | **hard kill** |
| `StallWatchdog`, `stall_after` = 900s | `lane_activity` = commits + dirty tree | **yes** | flag only |

`StallWatchdog`'s docstring and config.py:1408-1410 both state the flag-not-kill choice
deliberately: *"a slow-but-working run is never cut short."* That instinct is right, but it left
the wall clock as sole executioner - and the wall clock cannot distinguish a working lane from a
wedged one. So the harness **hard-kills lanes that are demonstrably working** and **merely files a
queue item for lanes that are demonstrably wedged.**

That inversion is why the deadline ends up calibrated at 95% of the real work distribution: it is
carrying a job it has no information to do.

## Second defect, independent of the first: the salvage is asymmetric

On timeout the code rescues *buffered stdout* (`_drain`) and does nothing about the *worktree*,
which is where the run's entire value is. The routing then names the worktree explicitly -
loop.py:705 blocks with "inspect the worktree and re-dispatch", supervise.py:2395 queues a stall -
so the harness knows the tree matters and still never preserves it.

16.4M tokens of already-correct code was discarded while a few kilobytes of log was carefully
retained. That asymmetry, not the timeout value, is what makes the failure total.

## Why a cooperative fix will not work

`_kill_tree` terminates then SIGKILLs after `KILL_GRACE_S`. Extending that grace, or signalling
earlier so the agent can commit, depends on a third-party CLI treating SIGTERM as "commit now".
`claude -p` gives no such contract. **The salvage has to be harness-side** to be reliable.

## A blind spot in the probe that must be closed before the idle bound can kill

`lane_activity` (supervise.py:2136) hashes `git rev-parse HEAD` plus `git status --porcelain`. A
lane running a long test suite, or thinking, writes nothing and reads as **idle**. So making the
current probe terminal at 900s would trade one wrong kill for another - it would kill a lane
running our own 52s-to-14min gate set if it happened to be quiet.

Before the idle bound becomes terminal, the observed quiet-interval tail has to be measured and the
threshold set above it - the same discipline `basicly-m4zv.14` used for `-n auto`. The probe may
also need widening beyond git state.

payload.description:
From spike basicly-zv48 dimension 2. `protect-generated.py` is a fail-open, Claude-specific PreToolUse hook: a tool-time bypass (or any non-Claude agent) can still stage a hand-edit to a basicly-generated file and reach a commit. Add a deterministic, agent-independent git backstop that catches it at commit time.

Design: a new pre-commit hook (`manager: git`, stdlib-only, companion to `protect-generated.py`) reads the projection manifest (`generated-manifest.json` -> `outputs` map of repo-relative path -> recorded sha256) and, for every staged generated OUTPUT whose staged blob no longer matches the hash the last `basicly build` recorded, blocks the commit. A legitimate rebuild stages the regenerated file AND the updated manifest together so hashes agree (pass); a hand-edit that skips the rebuild does not (block). Fail-safe: a missing manifest or unreadable git index exits 0 (a guardrail against accidents, not a security boundary — same stance as the PreToolUse guard).

## Acceptance Criteria

- A new pre-commit git hook blocks a commit that stages a basicly-generated output file whose staged content diverges from the projection manifest's recorded hash, naming the offending file(s) and pointing at the catalog-source + `basicly build` fix.
- A legitimate rebuild (regenerated output + updated manifest staged together) passes; a commit that stages no generated files passes; a staged deletion is not blocked (edits are the target).
- Fail-safe: a missing/unreadable manifest or a git-index read failure exits 0 (never locks a commit on the hook's own error).
- The hook is wired into `hooks.yaml` (`manager: git`, `stage: pre-commit`) and projected by `basicly hooks-build`; `basicly hooks-check` passes and the projected pre-commit config carries the entry.
- Full suite, ruff, ruff format, pyright, bandit, and the projection gates (basicly check / skills-check / agents-check / hooks-check) pass; verified by exercising a real commit (a hand-edited generated file is blocked; a clean tree commits).

## Notes

- The existing `protect-generated.py` PreToolUse guard stays as the first line (Claude tool-time); this hook is the deterministic commit-time backstop for all agents.
- Hash is compared over the staged blob bytes against the working-tree manifest (which reflects the last build); this mirrors `renderers.common.sha256_of_text` without importing basicly (hooks are standalone stdlib scripts copied to consumers).
payload.title: Guardrails: protect-generated git-stage manifest backstop

payload.description:
## Context

Backlog `docs/architecture/backlog.md` B3. The architecture document carries 16 mermaid blocks and the README one, and nothing checks that any of them renders. A block with a syntax error renders as a red error box on the hosting site and no gate here stops it landing.

The defect is not hypothetical. One revision named a `sequenceDiagram` participant `Loop`, which collides with mermaid's `loop` keyword. A parser caught it; review did not.

## Two corrections B3 carries, and both bind this work

A parse is the wrong instrument. Measured 2026-08-16 against mermaid 11 in a browser, `mermaid.parse()` accepts a `stateDiagram-v2` block whose transition label carries a second colon, and a renderer refuses the same block. The criterion is therefore *renders*, never *parses*.

And the reporting renderer could not be reproduced on mermaid 11, so which renderer the hosting surface uses is unestablished. The dependency is approved by the owner on 2026-08-21; establishing the hosting renderer and its version is part of this work, and the check records the renderer version it ran so a later mismatch is visible rather than silent.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN a tracked markdown file holds a mermaid block the renderer refuses, THE CHECK SHALL exit non-zero and name the file, the line, the renderer version and its message.
- WHEN every block renders, THE CHECK SHALL exit zero and print the block count and the renderer version.
- WHEN the renderer is not installed, THE CHECK SHALL fail rather than skip, because a skip reads as a pass.
- WHEN the tree holds no mermaid block at all, THE CHECK SHALL exit non-zero, because an empty population is the probe failing.

## Scope

- `.scripts/check_mermaid.py`
- `package.json`
- `package-lock.json`
- `tests/test_check_mermaid.py`
- `basicly.d/*.toml`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- budget: `120000`
- depends on: none
- demonstration: `uv run python .scripts/check_mermaid.py` reporting the tree block count and 0 failures, then exit 1 after a deliberate typo in one block.

From spike basicly-zv48 dimension 2. No redact/secret-scan logic exists anywhere. Add a blocking pre-commit gate so leaked credentials are caught deterministically. Chosen mechanism: a built-in stdlib scanner hook (no external dependency), distributed to consumers the way the other catalog hooks are.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A new stdlib-only core/hooks/secret-scan.py scans staged content at pre-commit and blocks the commit (non-zero exit) when a likely secret is detected, reporting file:line and the matched rule
- Detects common patterns: private-key headers, provider tokens (AWS, GitHub, Slack and similar), generic secret-named assignments, and dotenv-style KEY=<redacted:env-credential-assignment> secrets
- An inline suppression pragma lets a reviewed false positive through; only staged/added content is scanned
- hooks.yaml registers it (stage pre-commit, manager git); hooks-build wires it into .pre-commit-config.yaml and hooks-check verifies it; the repo dogfoods the active hook
- Deterministic tests cover each detection pattern, clean content passing, suppression, and staged-only scanning, with fixtures that build secrets by concatenation so committing the tests does not self-trip the hook
- pytest, ruff, pyright, and the projection gates stay green

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given the calibrated build factor when it is removed then every class factor is its working-set-shaped seed the turn multiplier is applied in exactly one ratio and a regression test fails if a spend-derived factor is ever compared against the working set ceiling
payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

```
uv run python -c "
from pathlib import Path
from basicly import decompose, config
s = config.load_sizing_config(Path('.'))
print('seeds     :', s.build_factors)
print('calibrated:', decompose.calibrated_build_factors(Path('.'), s))
print('band max  :', s.working_set_max)
"
```

Observed - `{'task': 216.65, 'bug': 2.0, 'chore': 1.5}` against seeds `{'task': 3.0, 'bug': 2.0, 'chore': 1.5}` and a `working_set_max` of 64000. Expected - a factor in the same order as its seed, because the ceiling it is compared against did not change.

## Context

`decompose.calibrated_build_factors` computes `factor = entry["tokens"] / scope_read_cost`, where `entry["tokens"]` is the dispatch's **whole-lane cumulative token spend** and the result is multiplied by scope cost and compared against `working_set_max = 64000`, a **context-window** bound. The two are different units. The seed 3.0 models a working set; the calibration replaces it with a spend ratio, and spend is three orders of magnitude larger.

The 20 real samples on this tree, `tokens / scope`:

| class | samples | factors (min..max) | median | seed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| task | 11 | 38.1 .. 2309.4 | **216.65** | 3.0 |
| bug | 7 | 198.0 .. 2310.1 | (seed kept) | 2.0 |
| chore | 2 | 432.2 .. 2013.0 | (seed kept) | 1.5 |

`calibration_min_samples` is 10, so only `task` has crossed the threshold. `bug` is at 7 - **three more bug dispatches and bugs are refused too**, then chore.

Consequences, all measured:

1. With factor 216.65 the largest scope that can pass is `64000 / 216.65` = about **295 tokens of scope read cost** before overhead. Every task-typed child with a scope beyond a couple of tiny files is refused permanently.
2. `basicly decompose <epic> --plan p.toml --dry-run` on a fresh 5-child epic (`basicly-uhiq`) returned `verdict: REFUSED` for 4 of 5 children. The only child that passed is the one typed `chore`, whose factor is still the seed.
3. The same factor feeds the spend forecast, which reported **$6408.66 and 13435 minutes** for a child whose real work is editing markdown.
4. The engine gets worse the more it is used: ten successful dispatches are what disabled the gate. This is a self-inflicted lockout, not a size problem.

This reframes the "size-debt deadlock" recorded in the handover. That deadlock was attributed to the size of `cli.py` (91,839) and `supervise.py` (71,222). For **bug**-typed work that attribution is right - `basicly-tcmy.9` sized at 75,648 = 37,082 x 2.0 + overhead, refused on file size alone. For **task**-typed work it is wrong: the refusals are the calibration, not the files.

Not a duplicate of `basicly-tcmy.5`, which covers the build factor's provenance and phase naming. This is a units defect in the calibration itself.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a calibrated build factor when it is computed then its numerator and the ceiling it is compared against are the same unit and a test fails if a spend-shaped numerator is compared to a working-set ceiling
- Given the twenty run records on this tree when the factors are calibrated then no class factor exceeds a bounded multiple of its seed and the bound is enforced rather than documented
- Given a five-child markdown-only epic when decompose dry-runs it then no child is refused for size and the forecast is within an order of magnitude of a real markdown lane
- Given a class that has not reached calibration_min_samples when more samples arrive then crossing the threshold cannot make a previously dispatchable child undispatchable without a recorded reason

## Scope

- `src/basicly/decompose.py`
- `src/basicly/config.py`
- `tests/test_decompose.py`
payload.title: The calibrated build factor divides whole-lane spend by scope cost so the size band refuses every task

payload.text:
BASELINE measured in base at 067ce1c BEFORE the fix, so the ACs are falsifiable at review.

DIAGNOSIS SHARPENED. forecast_spend's docstring states the invariant: 'the turn multiplier lives in exactly one ratio and the other two stay a price and a rate'. That ratio is tokens_per_working_set_token = 334. calibrated_build_factors computes whole-lane-spend / scope = 216, and whole-lane spend ALREADY contains the turn multiplier. So the multiplier is applied twice: 73603 x 216 x 334 = the 5.3 trillion token forecast. The calibration violates the invariant it was meant to serve.

The forecast PRICE is NOT defective - I initially divided cost by working set instead of by forecast tokens. Both children price at ~0.73 USD per million against a measured 0.848. Only the working-set estimate feeding it is wrong.

No run record carries a working-set measure (fields are tokens, cost, duration_s only), so the numerator cannot be corrected - hence delete rather than repair. Owner ruled: delete the calibration, keep the seeds.

BEFORE: factors {task 216.65, bug 2.0, chore 1.5}; task has 11 samples against calibration_min_samples 10; bug has 7 and chore 2, so both still hold their seeds. Three more bug dispatches breaks bugs the same way.

AFTER, predicted with seed factors against band max 64000 - THE FIX DOES NOT UNBLOCK EVERYTHING AND MUST NOT CLAIM TO:
  uhiq child0 de-reference code    scope  73603 x3.0 = 220809  STILL REFUSED
  uhiq child1 delete orphans       scope  12331 x1.5 =  18496  PASS
  uhiq child2 classify designs     scope 120667 x3.0 = 362001  STILL REFUSED
  uhiq child3 reconcile arch       scope  32519 x3.0 =  97557  STILL REFUSED
  uhiq child4 plan as index        scope  20311 x3.0 =  60933  PASS
Two of five pass. The other three refuse on honest scope read cost times seed factor - that is the real size-debt deadlock and it is a separate problem from this bead. An AC claiming the epic decomposes cleanly after this fix would be false.

z2wi's own scope is 46256 x2.0 = 92512, over the band, so this is a manual lane.

payload.description:
## Context

`basicly-kn4rip` landed the reporting half of the swallow: the seam now says `already recorded` instead of `recorded:`. It deliberately left the swallow itself, and named the reason - nothing in the ledger separates a deliberate re-record from a replay, so the intent has to come from the caller. `Draft.generation` is the mechanism and no write verb reaches it.

Scoped 2026-08-22 against a scratch ledger. The live tracker was not probed.

## The mechanism, and it already works

`Draft.generation` is declared at `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/events.py:450` with default `1`, read at exactly one place - `events.py:1334`, the skip - and reaches the id through `ids.evidence_id` at `ids.py:379-382`. It is **not hashed**; it is a visible suffix:

```python
suffix = digest if generation == 1 else f"{digest}-{generation}"
```

So `gen=1` gives `rec#ev-04bc122532` and `gen=2` gives `rec#ev-04bc122532-2`. `generation < 1` raises. Nine `Draft(` constructions in `src/basicly/write_verbs.py` and none carries the kwarg.

## Proved on a scratch ledger

Driving `status` open then blocked then open through the kit CLI: the third write appended nothing, the folded status stayed `blocked`, and the CLI raised. The same third write with `generation=2` landed at seq 4 and the fold moved to `open`. The reported label sequence reproduces identically.

## The constraint that decides the design

`tracker.scrub_ledger` re-derives every event's generation as the **dense occurrence count** of an identical `(record, kind, payload)` in file order (`src/basicly/tracker.py:789-797`, used at `:834`), and raises `TrackerDivergenceError` and rewrites nothing if any stored id fails to re-mint (`:838-842`). That runs on the commit path. So a caller flag may not mint an arbitrary generation - it must resolve to `occurrence_count + 1`, as `migrate.py:523` already does. The derivation was verified to reproduce a hand-written `gen=2` event.

## Which verbs need it

`update --status`, `update` label flags, `update` other fields, `close`, `dep add` and `gate report` all have a reachable A then B then A. `dep remove` is guarded by `_refuse_a_retraction_of_an_absent_edge`. `create` cannot collide, because the id is minted per call. `comments add` should keep the swallow, because an identical body is a genuine duplicate.

**`gate report` is worse than the others: it is a plain A then A.** Its payload is `{provenance, gate, provider, passed}` and carries neither the note nor the actor (`write_verbs.py:227-235`), so a gate that really runs twice and passes twice is recorded once.

## Where an unknown flag is refused today, and where it is not

`update` refuses an unknown flag loudly (`write_verbs.py:123-129`). `close`, `dep add`, `dep remove` and `gate report` **silently drop it**. So a misspelled repeat flag on those four degrades straight back into the swallow, and now invisibly, because the operator believes they asked for a re-record. A shape-level guard at the seam covers all verbs at once; `_refuse_a_write_that_records_nothing` (`owned_write.py:145`) is the precedent.

## Where it threads

The strip belongs in `owned_write.append` around `owned_write.py:276`, beside `_resolve_labels` - that is the one place holding the ledger lock, which a dense-occurrence resolver requires, and it means no translator changes at all. It must run **after** `_stamped` (`:280`), because stamping rewrites the provenance key and therefore the digest. A valueless flag matches the argv grammar's existing shape and needs no `VALUE_FLAGS` entry.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Build a throwaway ledger under a scratch directory. The kit CLI takes its ledger directory as its first positional exactly so it can point away from the live one: `uv run python .basicly/core/kit/tracker/cli.py create <dir> --prefix scratch --title probe --status open`
2. `... update <dir> <id> --status blocked`
3. `... update <dir> <id> --status open`
4. `... show <dir> <id>`

**Observed.** Step 3 appends nothing and raises `IndexError`. Step 4 reports `status = blocked` with 3 events.

**Control.** Appending the same draft with `generation=2` returns one event id ending `-2`, and the fold moves to `open` at 4 events - so the ledger is writable and the swallow is the digest, not a broken probe.

**Never probe the live ledger at `.basicly/ledger/`.** An append-only log has no undo and a throwaway record's tombstone is permanent.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN a caller means a re-record genuinely, THERE SHALL be a flag that says so, and the resulting event SHALL fold to the intended value.
- WHEN that flag is used, THE GENERATION SHALL resolve to the next dense occurrence of the identical event, so `tracker.scrub_ledger` re-mints every id and does not diverge.
- WHEN the flag is absent, THE BEHAVIOUR SHALL NOT change, and `test_replaying_the_same_drafts_appends_nothing` SHALL still pass unmodified.
- WHEN a verb that silently drops unknown flags is given a misspelled one, IT SHALL be refused rather than degrade into the swallow.
- WHERE the flag is not idempotent by construction, THAT SHALL be stated rather than hidden; running it twice appends twice, and making it idempotent would reintroduce the swallow.
- WHERE an engine path calls `tracker.write`, IT SHALL NOT pass the flag, because a state re-entered on every advance must still record one event.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/owned_write.py`
- `src/basicly/tracker_argv.py`
- `src/basicly/tracker_write.py`
- `tests/test_owned_write.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- budget: `130000`
- depends on: `basicly-kn4rip`
- demonstration: On a scratch ledger drive one field A then B then A with the flag and read back A, against two controls - the same sequence without the flag, which must still fold to B, and an identical replay run twice, which must append once.
payload.title: no write verb can say a re-record is deliberate so a field cannot return to a value it held

**`gate report` is worse than the others: it is a plain A then A.** Its payload is `{provenance, gate, provider, passed}` and carries neither the note nor the actor (`write_verbs.py:227-235`), so a gate that really runs twice and passes twice is recorded once.

## Where an unknown flag is refused today, and where it is not

`update` refuses an unknown flag loudly (`write_verbs.py:123-129`). `close`, `dep add`, `dep remove` and `gate report` **silently drop it**. So a misspelled repeat flag on those four degrades straight back into the swallow, and now invisibly, because the operator believes they asked for a re-record. A shape-level guard at the seam covers all verbs at once; `_refuse_a_write_that_records_nothing` (`owned_write.py:145`) is the precedent.

## Where it threads

The strip belongs in `owned_write.append` around `owned_write.py:276`, beside `_resolve_labels` - that is the one place holding the ledger lock, which a dense-occurrence resolver requires, and it means no translator changes at all. It must run **after** `_stamped` (`:280`), because stamping rewrites the provenance key and therefore the digest. A valueless flag matches the argv grammar's existing shape and needs no `VALUE_FLAGS` entry.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Build a throwaway ledger under a scratch directory. The kit CLI takes its ledger directory as its first positional exactly so it can point away from the live one: `uv run python .basicly/core/kit/tracker/cli.py create <dir> --prefix scratch --title probe --status open`
2. `... update <dir> <id> --status blocked`
3. `... update <dir> <id> --status open`
4. `... show <dir> <id>`

**Observed.** Step 3 appends nothing and raises `IndexError`. Step 4 reports `status = blocked` with 3 events.

**Control.** Appending the same draft with `generation=2` returns one event id ending `-2`, and the fold moves to `open` at 4 events - so the ledger is writable and the swallow is the digest, not a broken probe.

**Never probe the live ledger at `.basicly/ledger/`.** An append-only log has no undo and a throwaway record's tombstone is permanent.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN a caller means a re-record genuinely, THERE SHALL be a flag that says so, and the resulting event SHALL fold to the intended value.
- WHEN that flag is used, THE GENERATION SHALL resolve to the next dense occurrence of the identical event, so `tracker.scrub_ledger` re-mints every id and does not diverge.
- WHEN the flag is absent, THE BEHAVIOUR SHALL NOT change, and `test_replaying_the_same_drafts_appends_nothing` SHALL still pass unmodified.
- WHEN a verb that silently drops unknown flags is given a misspelled one, IT SHALL be refused rather than degrade into the swallow.
- WHERE the flag is not idempotent by construction, THAT SHALL be stated rather than hidden; running it twice appends twice, and making it idempotent would reintroduce the swallow.
- WHERE an engine path calls `tracker.write`, IT SHALL NOT pass the flag, because a state re-entered on every advance must still record one event.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/owned_write.py`
- `src/basicly/tracker_argv.py`
- `src/basicly/tracker_write.py`
- `tests/test_owned_write.py`
- `src/basicly/re_record.py`
- `tests/test_re_record.py`
- `.importlinter`
- `docs/architecture/architecture.md`
- `docs/plan/implementation-plan.md`

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- budget: `130000`
- depends on: `basicly-kn4rip`
- demonstration: On a scratch ledger drive one field A then B then A with the flag and read back A, against two controls - the same sequence without the flag, which must still fold to B, and an identical replay run twice, which must append once.

payload.description:
When a repository with basicly is worked from two machines on one branch, I want a shard arriving from the other machine folded at the merge, so I can keep the trunk log readable without waiting for the next landing.

The kit's post-merge hook cannot do this for a basicly repository: its commit carries no record id and tracker-commit-msg, written by the same install, refuses it, so it folds and leaves a dirty tree. That is why basicly-jmp6561 was withdrawn rather than shipped.

The engine already has what the hook lacks. commit_tracker_state folds and commits with an id the gate accepts, and merge_worktree calls it at the landing. What is missing is the same fold reached from a plain git merge or pull rather than only from a loop landing.

The gap is bounded and self-healing in an active repository: the next tracker write or landing folds whatever arrived. It is a quiet repository that accumulates, which is the canary's case between landings.
payload.requirements: no bypass of any gate: the commit carries a real record id rather than skipping the hook that asks for one. The engine reaches the fold through the seam it already uses rather than a second mechanism, and a repository without basicly keeps the kit's post-merge hook as its answer.

payload.description:
## Context

Observed 2026-08-20 by a lane during a nine lane pass. The session scratchpad is keyed by session, not
by lane, so **every concurrent subagent writes to one directory**.

The failure is silent substitution, which is worse than loss. A lane wrote a measurement script, a
sibling overwrote it between the write and the run, and the run **printed the sibling's files and
numbers under the first lane's command**. A shared backup directory held six other lanes' copies of
files, so a restore from backup would have written another lane's content into the wrong worktree.

The close out guidance already says anything worth keeping belongs in the repo rather than a temp
directory, and gives the reason as the scratchpad being cleaned without warning. Cross lane overwrite is
a second and worse reason: cleaning loses a file loudly, this substitutes one quietly, and no positive
control on the corpus catches it because the corpus was never wrong - the script was.

The blast radius is every number a lane measures through a scratchpad script, which in this repo means
every ratchet figure, every population count and every timing that reaches a commit message, a frozen
table or a design document.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Dispatch two or more concurrent lanes in one session.
2. Have each write a script of the same name into the scratchpad root and then run it.
3. Observe one lane's run execute the other lane's script, reporting the other lane's files and numbers with no error.
4. List the shared backup directory and observe files belonging to lanes other than the one reading it.
5. Observe a positive control on the measured corpus still passes, because the corpus is not what was swapped.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given two concurrent lanes when each writes a working file then neither can read or overwrite the other's - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_dispatch_brief.py -k scratch_isolation -q`
- Given a lane is briefed then it is told a working directory unique to it rather than a session wide path
- Given the close out guidance then it names cross lane substitution beside the cleaning hazard, because the two fail differently

## Scope

- `src/basicly/dispatch_brief.py`
- `tests/test_dispatch_brief.py`

## Working Set

- `src/basicly/dispatch_brief.py`
- `tests/test_dispatch_brief.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest -q`

payload.description:
The tool-usage PostToolUse hook (.basicly/core/hooks/tool-usage.py) is meant to count each shell command's pipeline heads, but it also records argument words and here-doc/commit-message body words as if they were command heads. In a real session it logged tokens like 'Refine', 'musical', 'portable', '--description', 'G_MODEL' alongside git/gh/br. This pollutes 'basicly usage report' with non-commands and makes the never-used-skill culling signal unreliable.

Root cause: tools_in_command() splits the raw command on pipeline operators (| && ; and newline) with a regex BEFORE tokenizing, so operators and newlines that appear INSIDE a quoted string (a multi-line 'git commit -m' body, a 'gh --title/--body' with a semicolon) shatter the quoted text into fake segments whose first word is then counted as a command head. Heredoc bodies are already stripped (basicly-587); quoted-string bodies are not.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run a command whose args include a multi-word quoted string with an operator or newline, e.g. 'git commit -m' with a multi-line body, or 'gh pr create --title "add x; ship it"', or a 'python3 - <<PY' heredoc.
2. Inspect .basicly/usage/tool-usage.json.
3. Observe body words (musical, portable, --description, ship) recorded as keys alongside the real commands.

## Acceptance Criteria

- tools_in_command() splits into pipeline segments in a quote-aware way: | && ; and newline that occur inside single/double quotes do NOT start a new segment, so quoted-string contents, flag values, and heredoc bodies are never counted.
- Only the real command at each pipeline head is counted; wrappers (uv/npx/...) still unwrap; builtins/env-assignments still skipped.
- Regression test covers a multi-line 'git commit -m' body AND a <<'PY' heredoc, asserting only the real commands are counted.
- Full test suite green.
payload.title: tool-usage hook counts heredoc/argument words as command heads

payload.description:
## Context

Owner 2026-08-22, reading the wall: *"in the board i only see 2 things in the loop: basicly-fi1i7z and basicly-rn0o.6"*.

Two lanes are drawn under `RUNNING NOW` and only **one** has an agent in it.

## The contract and the producer mean different things by the same word

`board-snapshot.schema.json`, what a consumer is promised:

> `live`: Whether the lane was still **running** when the snapshot was folded, as against last known to have been.

`supervise.AdoptedLane`, what the producer sets:

> True when the **worktree session record still exists on disk**; a bound issue whose worktree is gone needs a re-dispatch, not an adoption.

A worktree on disk is not a running agent. The producer answers a provisioning question and the schema promises an execution one.

## Measured on the live document

```text
basicly-rn0o.6   live true   tokens 3533746   note "Gate green. Now the demonstration..."   started 15:21:38Z
basicly-fi1i7z   live true   no tokens        no note                                      started 11:25:03Z
```

`fi1i7z` was adopted four hours before the reading, has never reported a token on this pass, and carries no activity line. The supervisor's own `running:` line names only `rn0o.6`. So the second card is a parked worktree drawn as work in flight.

## Why it reads worse than a missing field

An absent figure reads as absent. A **false** `live` reads as fact, and it is the field the region's whole meaning rests on: `RUNNING NOW` with two cards says two agents are working. The operator counted them and asked why the loop held only two things - the honest answer is that it holds one.

## The distinction the producer already has and does not use

`supervise.inflight_activity()` and `inflight_spend()` name exactly the lanes with a live stream, and `board_facts._lane_fact` already calls both - that is how `rn0o.6` gets its note and its tokens while `fi1i7z` gets neither. So the fact needed to tell the two apart is already in hand at the moment the card is built; it is simply not used to set `live`.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start a supervised pass, let one lane finish its dispatch while its worktree stays provisioned, and keep another running.
2. `curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8787/snapshot.json | jq '.lanes'`

**Observed.** Both carry `live: true`; only one carries `tokens` or a `note`, and only one appears on the supervisor's `running:` line.

**Control.** `jq '[.lanes[]|select(.note)]|length'` returns 1 against `jq '.lanes|length'` returning 2, so the producer can already distinguish them and the difference is not a reading artefact.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN a lane has no agent inside it, THE DOCUMENT SHALL NOT report it as running, and the region SHALL NOT draw it as work in flight.
- WHEN a lane is provisioned but idle, THAT STATE SHALL be expressible, because it is a real and useful state - a worktree waiting for a dispatch is not the same as a lane nobody has provisioned.
- WHEN the schema and the producer use one word for two facts, ONE OF THEM SHALL change, and the record SHALL say which and why rather than leaving both.
- WHERE the region is headed for what is running, ITS COUNT SHALL equal the number of agents actually running.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/board_facts.py`
- `src/basicly/board_sections.py`
- `tests/test_board_facts.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- budget: `100000`
- depends on: none
- demonstration: Run a pass with one lane dispatched and one provisioned-but-idle, and read the served document reporting one as running and one as idle, against the supervisor's own running line as the control.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a fresh consumer repo with basicly installed and no operator memory when an agent is asked to drive a supervised run then every fact it needs is available from a command a skill or the projected instructions and no step depends on knowledge that exists only in an agent private memory
payload.description:
## Context

Owner, 2026-08-01: **"If you need to go search your memory to run basicly correctly, we are doing
it wrong."** A consumer who installs basicly inherits the engine, the projected instructions, the
skills and the hooks — and none of an operator's accumulated recollection. So any knowledge required
to run basicly correctly that lives only in an agent's private memory is an undocumented runtime
dependency, and the consumer hits the failure the operator learned to avoid.

Externalize in this priority order, owner-specified:

1. **Deterministic** -> a script, a command, or a gate. The engine answers it; nobody recalls it.
2. **Semi-deterministic** -> a script plus a skill (the skill carries the judgment and references
   the script).
3. **Non-deterministic** -> instructions and skills.

## Audit, 2026-08-01

An operator memory of 58 entries was classified against what the repo actually enforces. Three
groups came out.

**Group A - required to run basicly, NOT externalized.** These are the defects.

- The **supervised-run runbook** does not exist in the catalog. `loop supervise` appears only in
  `docs/design/factory-design.md` and `docs/architecture/architecture.md` (which describe the
  system, not how to drive it) and in the `harness-client` skill (which is about attaching as a
  second observer). The `harness-loop` skill, 271 lines, barely mentions supervise, grants or
  budget. Everything about starting a run - mint a grant, size the budget from measured cost, check
  the base is clean, know which runner will meter spend - was operator memory.
- **`FORCE_COLOR` breaks the piped-output test: zero mentions anywhere in the repo.** Pure memory.
- Budget sizing from measured per-lane cost: the numbers exist in run records, but nothing reads
  them and says "a 5-lane pass needs about this much".
- `br` read patterns: `br list --json` caps at ~50 and drops closed rows, so a whole-tracker
  question must read `.beads/issues.jsonl`. A zero-finding audit was silently wrong once because of
  this.
- The tracker export re-adds `source_repo_path` on every write, so a scrub is required before
  staging. Loop landings scrub automatically; an out-of-loop write does not, and the operator
  remembers.

**Group B - required, and ALREADY externalized.** The memory entry is redundant history, which is
fine and needs no work: the loop landing guards (`4psl`, `9niw`, `o0q3`), the commit-message rules
(the `commit-msg` and `beads-commit-msg` hooks plus `basicly commit`), the lint rules (ruff,
markdownlint), the deny-list, `--all-default-roots`.

**Group C - not about running basicly.** Agent working discipline and project state: verification
habits, session history, measurements, Claude-Code-specific facts. These legitimately stay in an
agent's memory or a handover, and are out of scope here.

## Scope

Children, one per tier. Filed separately so each can be prioritized on its own.

- **Tier 1, done in this session**: `basicly-f3mi` (projected Claude hooks used a relative script
  path, so every consumer's hook broke outside the repo root - the exact defect an operator was
  papering over with a "never use a bare cd" note) and `basicly loop preflight <root>`, a read-only
  command that answers the whole pre-run checklist and exits non-zero when a run would be blocked.
- **Tier 1, remaining**: environment preconditions the engine should assert rather than an operator
  recall - `FORCE_COLOR`, the node resolution that differs in non-interactive shells, and an
  automatic export scrub on the out-of-loop `br` write path.
- **Tier 2**: a `harness-supervise` runbook skill (or a `harness-loop` section) that carries the
  judgment around a run and points at `loop preflight` for the facts.
- **Tier 3**: fold the verification-discipline rules into `test-discipline` and `harness-loop`.

## Measuring it

`.scripts/recall_eval.py` already measures whether an agent recalls the always-on baseline **with
every file read denied**, which is the right shape for this question: can an agent operate correctly
from what the repo projects and nothing else? Extending it to cover the operational runbook, rather
than only the always-on rules, is how this epic gets a number instead of an opinion.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a fresh consumer repo with basicly installed and no operator memory when an agent is asked
  to drive a supervised run then every fact it needs is available from a command, a skill or the
  projected instructions, and no step depends on knowledge that exists only in an agent's private
  memory

- When an agent follows the prompt in a repo with an existing settings file, it produces the classification table and the diff before any write.
- When the plan would remove or narrow a user entry or edit `.gitignore`, the agent stops for approval and changes nothing without it.

payload.description:
## Trigger

When a coding agent installs basicly into a repo, I want it to analyse the repo's existing agent settings before it merges anything, so I can get a merge fitted to what the repo already relies on, and not a mechanical union the agent cannot explain.

## Context

basicly has an agent install prompt for the tracker package only (`packages/basicly-tracker/README.md#install-with-a-coding-agent`, linked from README.md). Nothing guides an agent through installing basicly itself. The mechanical rule in basicly-f002zye cannot judge intent: whether a blanket allow is deliberate, whether a hand-added `ask` or deny (for example terminal's `git rebase*` deny) should stay, or whether `settings.local.json` entries are stale.

## Shape

- An agent install prompt (README section plus a skill) that runs, in order:
  1. `basicly install --dry-run --json`: a machine-readable plan per file and key, so the agent does not parse prose. This needs the `--json` form.
  2. Read `.claude/settings.json`, `.claude/settings.local.json`, the `.gitignore` rules for both, and the user-level `autoMode` block (read only).
  3. Classify every existing entry: kept as is, superseded by a managed entry, conflicts with a managed entry, risky (blanket allow, interpreter allow, absolute path), or stale (points at a path that no longer exists).
  4. Show the user one table of the entries it plans to change and why, with the proposed merged file as a diff. Wait for approval before it removes or narrows any user entry, or edits an ignore file.
  5. Run `basicly install`, then `permissions-check` and `hooks-check`, and report the backup path from basicly-f002zye.
- The agent never edits user-level settings. For auto mode it prints the proposed `autoMode` block (with `$defaults`) for the user to apply. The classifier refuses that edit as self-modification (observed 2026-09-25).
payload.requirements:
- The classification uses the same merge rule as basicly-f002zye. The prompt reads the `--json` plan; it does not restate the rule.
- Validate it as a consumer: a scratch repo seeded with the settings shapes from the parent record (blanket allow, ignored settings file, stale local allows).

## Trigger

When a person runs Claude Code in auto mode in a repository that basicly installed, I want the shipped permission rules to work in that mode, so I can work without prompts for routine read and check commands.

## Context

Tier 3 of basicly-ze8z: non-deterministic, so instructions and skills.

Four rules earned by repeated real incidents are currently only in an operator's memory. Each is a general discipline rather than a basicly fact, which is why they belong in a skill rather than a gate:

- **A closed blocker is not a working gate.** A closed bead proves the code exists, not that the gate binds. `jr0l.22` was shipped, tested and inert for 67% of the tracker, and reading it as discharged risk cost a 36% grant overrun. Probe the gate's own functions against the real inputs first; a gate that fails open on missing input reports success indistinguishably from one that passed.
- **A broad test break is a layer error.** When one edit reddens many tests, read three of them before touching either side: they are collectively describing an invariant of the layer you reached into. Fourteen tests went red on a probe placed one layer too low; moving it fixed all fourteen with no assertion loosened.
- **Print the sample before choosing an estimator.** Two of three attempts at a spend bound were refuted by the data, not by argument: the population was bimodal, so any high quantile bounded cheap work using expensive work.
- **A capability fix can arm a pre-existing safety hole.** Removing a manual step removes whatever that step was implicitly authorizing. Letting the supervisor seed its own lanes put an ungranted session - which had no spend ceiling at all - one command from dispatching five metered agents.

Homes: the first three fit `test-discipline` and `harness-loop`; the fourth is a review habit and fits `harness-loop` or `session-finish`. Author as catalog YAML per the `catalog-authoring` skill, never a discoverable .md.

## Trigger

When a hand-built fixture encodes the format its author believes in rather than the format itself, I want `test-discipline` to require a test that drives a live capture where one exists in the tree, so I can catch a parser defect a hand-built fixture cannot see.

## Context

Session 2026-08-14, `basicly-ejdm.2`. Nine unit tests over hand-built transcript turns all passed
against a pairing rule that was **wrong on every real transcript**. The demonstration caught it,
not the suite.

The rule paired a turn's tokens against the immediately preceding line. A real claude transcript
forwards the tool result as a `user` event carrying no usage, which sits between the call and the
turn that pays for the answer:

```text
assistant  tokens= 26234 tools=[Agent]   <- the call
user       tokens=     0 tools=[]        <- the forwarded result, no usage
assistant  tokens=     0 tools=[]
assistant  tokens= 26635 tools=[]        <- the turn that pays for the answer
```

So the rule reported a real captured lane as **100% unattributed** - a confident figure measuring
nothing. Every hand-built fixture had an assistant turn adjacent to its predecessor, because that
is the shape a person writes when they are thinking about the rule rather than the format.

`test-discipline` covers isolation, order-independence and asserting on observable behaviour. All
nine tests satisfied every one of those and were still blind, because the defect was in the

capture. Driving it took one scratch script.

payload.description:
## Trigger

When a lane finishes a task, I want its session held open for the next one instead of torn down, so I can pay the cache write once rather than once per task.

## Requirements

R1. A second task in a held session costs materially less than the same task in a fresh one, and the saving is measured rather than assumed.
R2. A session that cannot start its next task inside the host's cache window is ended, because an idle held session is worse than a fresh one.
R3. A held session is releasable at any moment without losing work, because everything that must survive it is already written.
R4. A crash of a held session loses no more than a fresh dispatch would.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When a seat finishes a task and another ready task matches it, then the engine resumes the same session rather than starting a new one. [check: `tests/test_seat.py`]
- When a seat has no matching ready task and the cache window is about to close, then the engine releases the seat. [check: `tests/test_seat.py`]
- When a seat is released, then no unwritten state is lost, because the release happens only at a task boundary. [check: `tests/test_seat.py`]
- When a seat run is recorded, then the run record names the seat, the task's position in it, and the cache window in force. [check: `tests/test_run_record.py`]

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_seat.py -q`

## Design notes

Architecture section 31A.1, 31A.2 and D-46. Measured 2026-09-13 on five live dispatches, recorded on basicly-8724lqq: a warm session cost 0.20x and 0.19x of a fresh one on two replications at the same token count, and the saving is the avoided cache write rather than fewer tokens. Two limits carry into this work: two turns per task, and a cold resume past the window is unpriced.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `uv run basicly board serve --port 8787`
2. `curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8787/ > <redacted:posix-absolute-path>`
3. `uv run python .scripts/check_render_overflow.py --width 1440 --height 900 <redacted:posix-absolute-path>`

Observed on 2026-09-07: `body: 0px wider, 152px taller than its box` at 1440x900, and `49px` at 1600x1000. Clean at 1920x1080. The body is `100vh` with `overflow: hidden`, so those pixels are drawn and never seen - the footer's agents line and part of the inventory row fall off with no scrollbar to say so.

## Why the served page and not the written one

`board --out --width W --height H` is clean at all three sizes. `board serve` is told no viewport, so `board_regions.next_up` takes the conservative default for an unstated one and sizes the ready list for a taller page than the reader has. The default is conservative in the wrong direction.

## Measured against a control

Rendered one snapshot through the template at `90bffd1d~1` and at `HEAD`: 152px and 154px at 1440x900. So this is not the titles change of `basicly-lc2bd3v.8`; it predates it, and that change costs 2px.

This is not `basicly-c9crxu`, which is about the *narrow* ready column ignoring the viewport while lanes are running. This one has no lane running and the whole page overflows.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN the board is served and no viewport is declared, THE PAGE SHALL fit the reader's viewport at 1440x900, 1600x1000 and 1920x1080.
- WHERE the server cannot know the viewport, THE PAGE SHALL size its capped list from the shortest viewport the layout claims to support, not the tallest.
- THE FIX SHALL NOT reintroduce a scrollbar on the wall: the page is read across a room and nobody scrolls it.
- A CHECK SHALL measure the served bytes, not only the `--out` artifact, because the two differ in exactly the input this record is about.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/board_regions.py`
- `src/basicly/board_serve.py`
- `tests/test_board_regions.py`
- `changelog.d/<this-id>.fixed.md`

## Plan

- integrity: `L1`
- budget: `60000`
- depends on: none
- demonstration: serve the board and run the overflow instrument against the served bytes at all three viewports

payload.description:
## Context

Six lanes in one pass on 2026-08-22 were each blocked from committing by the `release-notes` gate reporting changelog entries that belong to **other** records and are present on main. The gate is right every time and none of the lanes did anything wrong.

## The loop, and it closes

```text
the supervisor requires a clean base to land          (base: clean, checked every round)
  -> a tracker write dirties the base                 (.basicly/ledger/events-*.jsonl)
  -> so the tracker write must be committed to main
  -> main advances
  -> every in-flight branch is now behind main
  -> release-notes reports main's changelog entries as missing from the branch
  -> the branch cannot commit
  -> it needs a rebase, which is on the explicit-confirmation list
  -> so it escalates to a human
```

Every step is correct in isolation. The cycle is the defect.

## Measured on this pass

Thirteen commits reached main while six lanes were in flight. Five landings were held behind a pass-level flag set by the first failure. Two lanes escalated a decision asking permission to rebase - `basicly-fi1i7z` explicitly, and `basicly-6oa3mt` hit the same wall while committing. Two branches additionally acquired a merge commit from trying `git merge main` instead, which `rebase.merge_commits` refuses at landing, so that route strands the lane rather than saving it.

The gate already distinguishes the two cases correctly and says so in its own words: *this tree is behind, not in debt. Rebase. Never declare it invisible - such an entry is true at a branch point and false on arrival.* So the diagnosis is not the gap; the **remedy is gated on a human** and the human is the same actor whose commits caused it.

## Three candidate cuts, and the evidence for each

**Rebase a lane's own branch without a human.** A rebase of an unlanded, unpushed, lane-owned branch onto its own base rewrites no shared history. The confirmation rule exists for published history and for destructive resets. Narrowing it to exclude this case removes the escalation entirely. Against: the rule is currently spelled by shape rather than by reach, so narrowing it needs the reach to be checkable - unpushed and unlanded are both testable.

**Let the landing rebase.** The engine already rebases at landing (`rebase.merge_commits` is its own refusal), so the capability is present; what is missing is doing it *before* the lane's own commit rather than at the merge queue.

**Stop advancing main during a pass.** The tracker's own writes are the only thing forcing it. If the base's cleanliness check ignored the ledger - which the engine commits itself at provisioning, landing and ship - a session's tracker writes would not have to reach main mid-pass at all.

The third is the root cut and the first is the cheap one. They are not exclusive.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start a supervised pass with two or more lanes.
2. While they run, close any record whose `## Scope` names a shipped path, write its `changelog.d/<id>.<category>.md`, and commit that to main.
3. Wait for a lane to finish and attempt its own commit.

**Observed 2026-08-22.** The lane's commit is refused by `release-notes` naming a changelog file it has never heard of, its verify reports 31 of 32, and it can neither commit nor rebase without a human.

**Control.** The same lane on a branch forked after that commit passes `release-notes` unchanged, so the refusal is the base gap and not the lane's own debt.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN a lane's branch is behind its base and owes nothing itself, IT SHALL be able to reach a committable state without a human decision.
- WHEN the base advances during a pass, THE COST SHALL be bounded, and a lane SHALL NOT be refused for a record it has no relationship to.
- WHEN a lane resolves being behind, IT SHALL NOT be able to do so by creating a merge commit the landing gate will later refuse.
- WHERE a human decision is genuinely required, THE ESCALATION SHALL name a remedy the lane is permitted to run.
- WHERE the ledger is the only thing dirtying the base, THAT SHALL be reconsidered, because the engine already owns committing it at three other points.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `tests/test_supervise.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- budget: `130000`
- depends on: none
- demonstration: Run a two-lane pass, advance main mid-pass with a closed record carrying a changelog entry, and watch both lanes reach a committed state with no human decision, against a control run on the current engine where they do not.
payload.title: advancing main during a pass refuses every in flight lane and the remedy needs a human

payload.text:
[recurred the same day 2026-08-22] Filed this morning after six lanes were refused, and I walked back into it after lunch. I said I would freeze main while lanes ran and then committed to it five more times - the always-on rule, its changelog, the fable design records, a scope correction and a gate-edge fix.

Measured now: harness/basicly-rn0o-6 is four commits behind main, and main carries changelog.d/basicly-grpzkw.changed.md, which is a closed record the lane cannot see. Its next commit will be refused by release-notes for a record it has no relationship to, which is the exact shape this record describes.

That is the second occurrence in one day, so this is a design defect rather than an operator lapse - the loop closes whether or not the operator remembers. The evidence is now two instances rather than one, and the second happened to someone who had just written the first down.

It also sharpens which of the three candidate cuts is right. Discipline is not a cut: I had the rule, wrote it, and broke it within three hours. The root cut is the third one on this record - the base's cleanliness check should not force a session's tracker writes onto main mid-pass, because the engine already owns committing the ledger at provisioning, landing and ship.
